 After smooth election, Wisconsin clerks look to Legislature for long-sought changes
 Legislation allowing absentee ballot processing ahead of election day tops the list. Incoming Democratic leaders have previously supported it
 By Rich Kremer 
 November 12, 2026 
 Updated 
 November 12, 2026 at 
 9:13 am 
 Workers count absentee ballots at the Wisconsin Center for the midterm election Tuesday, Nov. 8, 2022, in Milwaukee. Morry Gash/AP Photo 
 Despite a smooth midterm, Wisconsin clerks say they still want changes to some election laws, and they’re eager to work with the new Legislature to get them passed. 
 In particular, clerks want to be able to process absentee ballots ahead of election day, an idea Wisconsin’s Democratic legislative leaders have previously supported.
There were no major issues at polling places during last week’s election, Wisconsin Elections Commission Administrator Meagan Wolfe told reporters during a Wednesday press conference. She also said there appeared to be fewer issues with U.S. Postal Service deliveries of absentee ballots than in previous elections.
After Wolfe lauded Wisconsin’s army of local elections clerks for their hard work, Kim Trueblood, the Marathon County clerk, and Karla Endres, president of the Wisconsin Municipal Clerks Association, pitched changes they’d like to see from state lawmakers to make future elections even smoother.
Endres said clerks are looking to work with the Legislature to pass what’s known as a “Monday processing” bill, a concept that has garnered bipartisan support in the past but has been unable to clear previous Republican majorities. Endres referenced a federal investigation into letters with white powder being sent last month to the Wisconsin Elections Commission and other election offices nationwide.
“This would alleviate us from having that in the polls on election day, and potentially creating a bigger incident,” Endres said. 
The idea behind the Monday processing pitch is to allow clerks to process absentee ballots the day before an election in order to speed up the counting on election day. It gained steam after President Donald Trump and his supporters falsely claimed big shifts in election results late in the night from cities like Milwaukee were the result of fraud.
 With Democrats winning majorities in the state Senate and Assembly and holding the governor’s office, clerks have reason to be optimistic about Monday processing becoming a reality next year. That’s because the Legislature’s incoming Democratic leaders — Sen. Dianne Hesselbein , D-Middleton, and Rep. Greta Neubauer, D-Racine, both cosponsored such legislation last year and Gov.-elect David Crowley has said he supports the proposal .

 Trueblood also said a current requirement for poll workers to write a voter’s poll list number on their absentee ballot should be lifted because it could potentially reveal who a person voted for.
“If someone were to give us an open records request for ballot images, and then also request a poll book, they could very easily tie a person to their ballot,” Trueblood said. “Those of us who have gotten those requests in the past have spent many, many hours redacting those voter numbers from ballot images before releasing them, just to avoid the possibility of anyone being able to make that connection from the voter to their ballot.”
 Democrats did introduce a bill to lift the voter number requirement, which was cosponsored by Hesselbein, but Republicans blocked it. 
Neither Hesselbein nor Neubauer immediately responded to a request for comment on whether they plan to pursue the election changes requested by clerks in the coming session. A spokesperson for Crowley said he’s focusing on building his transition team and looks forward to working with legislative leadership “to advanced shared priorities that deliver results for Wisconsinites.”
